transcript: Convenience saves time, but it can also hide the decisions we are making. A delivery button removes the walk to a shop, a recommendation removes the search, and an automatic renewal removes the moment when we ask whether a service still matters. None of those tools is automatically harmful. The cost appears when speed becomes the only value we measure. We may spend more money, create more waste, or stop discovering alternatives. A useful response is to keep convenience for repetitive tasks while adding deliberate pauses before expensive or lasting choices. That balance preserves the benefit without allowing every quick option to become the default.
